Pregnancy

Second-trimester miscarriage: causes and follow-up

Updated: November 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Losing a pregnancy after the first trimester can leave you searching for an explanation, especially if earlier checks seemed reassuring. Several different pathways can lead to a loss at this stage. Reviewing what happened can sometimes identify a condition that changes future care, but tests do not always provide a definite answer. A risk factor or an uncertain result is not proof that you caused the loss.

First clarify what the terms mean

Second-trimester miscarriage is also called a late miscarriage or mid-trimester loss, but the week boundaries differ between countries and clinical guidelines. In the UK, miscarriage means a pregnancy loss before 24 completed weeks; the NHS describes late miscarriage as occurring from 14 through 23 weeks. Other services use different thresholds. Ask which definition applies to your records and care.

Stillbirth describes a baby dying before birth at or beyond the locally defined threshold. Neonatal death means death after a baby is born alive; it is not another name for miscarriage after a particular week. These distinctions help services arrange appropriate care and review. They do not measure the importance of your baby or how much support you deserve.

The sequence of events helps guide the investigation

Tell the reviewing clinician what happened first: bleeding, pain, pressure, leaking fluid, contractions, a scan finding or an illness. A cervix that opened with little pain, waters that broke before labour and a baby found to have died on ultrasound may lead to different questions. Sometimes several processes occur together, making it difficult to identify which started the problem.

The team combines this history with examination findings, ultrasound records and laboratory results. Symptoms alone cannot establish the cause, and an abnormal test may be unrelated to the loss. Ask whether a finding is a likely explanation, a possible contributor or something whose significance remains uncertain. This is more useful than assuming that every result outside a reference range needs treatment.

Chromosomes and development can matter, but are not the whole story

A chromosome change or a serious developmental condition can contribute to a later miscarriage. However, the causes of early miscarriage cannot simply be carried over to every second-trimester loss. Research populations and testing methods differ, so a single proportion cannot tell you whether a chromosome problem explains your pregnancy. Ask whether genetic testing could answer a specific question in your case.

A structural condition is not necessarily inherited, and conditions present before birth range from mild to very serious. Some have genetic causes, some involve other factors, and many remain unexplained. Screening estimates the likelihood of certain conditions; it does not diagnose every possible problem. If testing suggests a genetic explanation, counselling can clarify what the result means and whether parental testing would help.

Cervical and uterine factors need their own assessment

The cervix normally stays closed during pregnancy. Cervical insufficiency describes opening too early, often with little pain and without established labour. A short cervix on a scan is a risk finding, but does not by itself prove cervical insufficiency or explain a previous loss. Previous cervical surgery, some birth injuries and the pattern of earlier pregnancies can influence the assessment.

Some uterine shapes, such as a septate or bicornuate uterus, may also be relevant. Imaging may help clarify the anatomy. Neither a cervical procedure nor an unusual uterine shape means that miscarriage is inevitable. In another pregnancy, specialist review may lead to cervical scans, selected progesterone treatment or a stitch, depending on the history and findings. These options are not automatically appropriate after every later loss.

Placental findings may explain part of what happened

The placenta supports oxygen and nutrient transfer to the baby. Problems affecting its attachment or function can contribute to pregnancy loss. Placental abruption means separation from the uterine wall before birth; it can cause pain, bleeding and contractions. It is one possible explanation, not a universal leading cause of second-trimester miscarriage, and symptoms should not be dismissed because they occur before the final weeks.

Examination of the placenta, cord and membranes after a loss may reveal inflammation, bleeding or changes in blood flow. A finding still needs to fit the pregnancy history. Ask what the pathology report establishes and what it cannot prove. High blood pressure, an injury or a previous placental problem may affect the assessment without identifying a definite cause on their own.

Infection is possible; a vaginal result does not prove causation

Infection or inflammation involving the membranes, placenta or fluid around the baby can contribute to a later loss. Sometimes there was fever or illness; sometimes the concern emerges from laboratory or placental findings. The team decides which tests are useful from symptoms, exposures and the circumstances. A list of vaginal infections cannot establish which, if any, affected an individual pregnancy.

Bacterial vaginosis is associated with some adverse pregnancy outcomes, and symptomatic infection during pregnancy needs clinical assessment and appropriate treatment. That is different from screening everyone without symptoms to prevent preterm birth: studies have produced mixed results, and routine screening for this purpose is not recommended by CDC guidance. Do not start antibiotics or vaginal remedies yourself, or assume that a past infection proves why the loss occurred.

Review ongoing health conditions without assigning blame

Diabetes, thyroid disease, high blood pressure and autoimmune conditions deserve review when planning care. Their relevance depends on the particular condition, disease activity, treatment and pregnancy findings. Well-controlled diabetes or thyroid disease should not simply be labelled the cause of a miscarriage. A diagnosis such as polycystic ovary syndrome, or a risk association reported in a study, is not an individual explanation.

Bring your medication list and relevant clinic records to follow-up. Ask whether any condition needs better assessment or a different pregnancy plan. Do not stop prescribed treatment because you fear it caused the loss; uncontrolled illness can also create risks. A clinician can explain which changes are supported by your results and which proposed treatments lack evidence for your situation.

Antiphospholipid syndrome differs from inherited clotting conditions

Antiphospholipid syndrome, or APS, is an acquired immune-related condition associated with blood clots and certain pregnancy complications. It is distinct from inherited thrombophilias and from a diagnosis of lupus alone. Selected antibody tests may be appropriate after a later loss, but one positive result does not establish APS. Clinical history, test timing and repeat results matter.

Inherited thrombophilia tests are not a routine answer to every miscarriage, and weak associations do not show that blood thinners will prevent another loss. Specialists may consider particular tests when the wider history would change care. Aspirin or heparin may be indicated for specific circumstances, including established obstetric APS, but should not be started or stopped without your clinician. A painful, swollen or red leg needs urgent assessment for a possible clot, rather than waiting for a thrombophilia test.

Injury and substance exposure deserve care, not assumptions

An abdominal injury can affect the pregnancy, including through placental separation, but many incidents do not cause a loss. The force, injuries, gestation and assessment all matter. Seek prompt medical advice after a fall or abdominal blow and immediate assessment after a road crash. If someone hurt you, ask to speak privately with a healthcare professional when safe; you deserve support and protection.

Cocaine and amphetamines can affect placental blood flow, and cocaine has been linked with abruption. Evidence about other exposures varies and is often complicated by additional factors. Tell your clinician about alcohol, tobacco, recreational drugs and medicines so care can be tailored. An exposure history does not prove causation. If you use drugs regularly, seek medical help with stopping; abrupt withdrawal from some drugs can be dangerous.

Ask what each proposed investigation could change

A review may include the pregnancy records, placental examination, genetic testing, selected blood tests and imaging of the uterus. Not everyone needs every investigation. Ask what question each test addresses, whether its timing matters and how a positive or negative result would affect care. Some blood tests need repeating after recovery, and some results take weeks or longer to return.

Examination of the baby may also be offered, with discussion of consent, available options and limitations. It is separate from a single tissue sample or genetic test. You can ask for a trained professional to explain the choices at a pace you can manage. An investigation that provides no definite cause is not evidence that the loss was imaginary or that a parent was responsible.

Plan follow-up after one later loss

You do not have to assume that a specialist discussion is available only after several miscarriages. RCOG guidance includes one or more second-trimester losses. Ask who will review the results with you, when to expect an appointment and whom to contact while waiting. The discussion should include physical recovery, emotional wellbeing and any unanswered questions, even if you do not want another pregnancy.

If you do want to become pregnant again, arrange a review before trying or early in pregnancy. The plan may address a specific health condition, cervical monitoring, placental concerns or additional support. A previous later loss can increase risk, but does not make recurrence inevitable. Published averages cannot predict your individual outcome, and neither finding a cause nor following a plan guarantees prevention.

Current symptoms should not wait for the cause review

During pregnancy, contact maternity care promptly for bleeding, leaking fluid, new pelvic pressure or persistent pain. Fever, foul-smelling discharge or worsening pain during recovery also needs immediate medical advice. If your baby's movements have become established and then reduce or change, contact the maternity team immediately. These symptoms need assessment; they do not automatically mean a miscarriage has occurred.

Use emergency care for heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, collapse, chest pain or difficulty breathing. Bleeding with shoulder pain or faintness also needs emergency help. Tell the service that you are pregnant or recently had a pregnancy loss. Do not wait for scheduled tests or a follow-up appointment when you feel seriously unwell. Ask your usual team for bereavement support as well as medical follow-up.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Interpret the history, gestation and investigation findings together rather than diagnosing a cause from one risk factor.

Use targeted evaluation and distinguish APS from inherited thrombophilia; treatment requires an individual indication.

Arrange follow-up and cause-directed future care after a later loss, while explaining uncertainty and avoiding guarantees.

How BeMama can help

Use this guide to prepare questions about the records, tests and follow-up plan. BeMama cannot determine why a pregnancy ended, interpret an individual pathology result or prescribe preventive treatment.

When to seek help

Seek prompt maternity advice for bleeding, fluid loss, persistent pain or new pressure, and immediate advice for fever or worsening recovery symptoms. Heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, collapse, chest pain or difficulty breathing needs emergency care. Bleeding with shoulder pain or faintness also needs emergency help; do not wait for follow-up tests.

Evidence notes updated: November 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Later miscarriage has several possible pathways; the sequence of events helps guide the review.
  • A risk factor, an association or an abnormal result does not by itself prove the cause.
  • Cervical, placental, genetic, infectious and maternal findings need individual interpretation.
  • APS is distinct from inherited thrombophilia; tests and blood thinners are not automatic.
  • Ask for follow-up after one later loss and an individual future-care plan without guarantees.

Frequently asked questions

Can an infection cause a second-trimester miscarriage?

An infection involving the pregnancy can contribute to a loss. However, a vaginal infection or positive swab alone does not prove that it caused the miscarriage. Symptoms, clinical findings and appropriate tests must be interpreted together. Seek care for current symptoms rather than treating yourself.

Can a blow to the abdomen cause a loss?

An injury can affect the placenta or pregnancy, but harm is not inevitable. Contact a healthcare professional promptly after a fall or direct blow, and seek immediate assessment after a road crash. Serious injury, severe pain, heavy bleeding or collapse requires emergency care.

Are chromosome problems the most common cause at this stage?

They can be a cause, but figures for early miscarriage cannot simply be applied to all later losses. Other pathways become important, and studies differ. Genetic testing may help in an individual case; a normal screening result does not exclude every genetic or developmental condition.

Are placental problems always the main explanation?

No. Placental dysfunction, separation or inflammation may contribute, but there is no single explanation for every second-trimester loss. Examination of the placenta can help when its findings are considered alongside the clinical history and other investigations.

Do I need a cervical stitch in another pregnancy?

Not automatically. The circumstances of the loss, previous cervical procedures and current findings guide specialist advice. Cervical scans, progesterone or a stitch may be appropriate in selected situations. A short cervix and cervical insufficiency are related concepts, but not interchangeable diagnoses.

Should I take aspirin or heparin to prevent another miscarriage?

Only if your clinician recommends it for a defined indication. APS, inherited thrombophilia and an isolated antibody result are different findings. The choice depends on your history, confirmed results and other risks; do not start, stop or alter prescribed treatment on your own.

What if all the investigations are inconclusive?

You should still receive a discussion of what was checked, what remains uncertain and what support or monitoring is appropriate. An unexplained loss does not establish blame. Ask for a written follow-up plan and early specialist contact if another pregnancy occurs.

Must I wait for another loss before asking for specialist advice?

No. One second-trimester loss can justify a cause-directed review and planning for future care. Referral pathways vary locally, so ask your maternity team or usual clinician who should review the records and outstanding results.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
